facts.statement: Nigersaurus lived during the Aptian to Albian stages of the Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Aptian – Albian

facts.statement: Nigersaurus was discovered in the Elrhaz Formation at Gadoufaoua in Niger.
facts.quote: It was discovered in the Elrhaz Formation in an area called Gadoufaoua, in Niger.

facts.statement: Fossils of Nigersaurus were first described in 1976, but the species was formally named in 1999.
facts.quote: Fossils of this dinosaur were first described in 1976, but it was only named Nigersaurus taqueti in 1999 after further and more complete remains were found and described.

facts.statement: The specific name taqueti honors Philippe Taquet, who discovered the first remains.
facts.quote: the specific name honours the palaeontologist Philippe Taquet, who discovered the first remains.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus was small for a sauropod, measuring 9 to 14.1 meters in length with a short neck.
facts.quote: Small for a sauropod, Nigersaurus was about 9 - 14.1 m long, and had a short neck.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus weighed approximately 1.9 to 4 metric tons, comparable to a modern elephant.
facts.quote: It weighed around 1.9 - 4 MT, comparable to a modern elephant.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus had a wide muzzle containing over 500 teeth that were replaced approximately every 14 days.
facts.quote: It had a wide muzzle filled with more than 500 teeth, which were replaced at a rapid rate: around every 14 days.

facts.statement: The tooth-bearing bones of Nigersaurus jaws were rotated transversely so that all teeth were located far to the front, unlike other tetrapods.
facts.quote: Unlike other tetrapods, the tooth-bearing bones of its jaws were rotated transversely relative to the rest of the skull, so that all of its teeth were located far to the front.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus had a highly pneumatized skeleton filled with air spaces, but possessed robustly built limbs.
facts.quote: Its skeleton was highly pneumatised (filled with air spaces connected to air sacs), but the limbs were robustly built.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus belongs to the subfamily Rebbachisaurinae of the family Rebbachisauridae within the sauropod superfamily Diplodocoidea.
facts.quote: Nigersaurus and its closest relatives are grouped within the subfamily Rebbachisaurinae (formerly thought to be grouped in the eponymous Nigersaurinae) of the family Rebbachisauridae, which is part of the sauropod superfamily Diplodocoidea.

facts.statement: The olfactory region of Nigersaurus's brain was underdeveloped, though its overall brain size was comparable to other dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The region of its brain that detected smell was underdeveloped, although its brain size was comparable to that of other dinosaurs.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Nigersaurus habitually held its head downwards or horizontally like other sauropods.
facts.quote: There has been debate on whether its head was habitually held downwards, or horizontally like other sauropods.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus lived in a riparian habitat and likely ate soft plants like ferns, horsetails, and angiosperms.
facts.quote: It lived in a riparian habitat, and its diet probably consisted of soft plants, such as ferns, horsetails, and angiosperms.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus remained poorly known until additional material was found during expeditions led by Paul Sereno in 1997 and 2000.
facts.quote: Although a common genus, the dinosaur had been poorly known until more material of other individuals was discovered during expeditions led by American palaeontologist Paul Sereno in 1997 and 2000.

facts.statement: The Nigersaurus fossils are housed at the National Museum of Niger.
facts.quote: These fossils are housed at the National Museum of Niger.

facts.statement: Among sauropods, Nigersaurus was small with a body length of 9 to 14.1 meters, a femur of 1 meter, and a weight of 1.9 to 4 metric tons.
facts.quote: Among that clade, Nigersaurus was fairly small, with a body length of only 9 - 14.1 m and a femur reaching only 1 m; it may have weighed around 1.9 - 4 MT, comparable to a modern elephant.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus had a short neck for a sauropod consisting of thirteen cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: It had a short neck for a sauropod, with thirteen cervical vertebrae.

facts.statement: The Nigersaurus skull was delicate with four side fenestrae larger than those in other sauropodomorphs.
facts.quote: The skull of Nigersaurus was delicate, with the four side fenestrae (openings in the skull) larger than in other sauropodomorphs.

facts.statement: The connecting bone struts in the Nigersaurus skull were usually less than 2 mm thick.
facts.quote: These connecting struts of bones were usually less than 2 mm thick.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus possessed a closed supratemporal fenestra, a unique trait among sauropodomorphs.
facts.quote: Another unique trait it had among sauropodomorphs was a closed supratemporal fenestra.

facts.statement: The maxillary tooth row of Nigersaurus was entirely transversely rotated, with the rear 90° everted towards the front.
facts.quote: The maxillary tooth row was in its entirety transversely rotated, its normal rear 90° everted towards the front.

facts.statement: No other tetrapod has all its teeth located as far forward as those of Nigersaurus due to its unique jaw configuration.
facts.quote: Due to this configuration, no other tetrapod had all of its teeth located as far to the front as Nigersaurus.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus had dental batteries with 68 columns in the upper jaws and 60 in the lower, totaling over 500 active and replacement teeth.
facts.quote: With 68 columns in the upper jaws and 60 columns in the lower jaws, these so-called dental batteries (also present in hadrosaurs and ceratopsians) comprised a total of more than 500 active and replacement teeth.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus is the only known tetrapod with jaws wider than the skull and teeth extending laterally across the front.
facts.quote: Nigersaurus is the only known tetrapod animal to have had jaws wider than the skull and teeth that extended laterally across the front.

facts.statement: Teeth similar to Nigersaurus have been found on the Isle of Wight and in Brazil, but their taxonomic affiliation remains unknown.
facts.quote: Teeth similar to those of Nigersaurus have been found on the Isle of Wight and in Brazil, but it is unknown whether they belonged to relatives of this taxon, or to titanosaurs, whose remains have been found in the vicinity.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus vertebrae contained little to no cancellous bone, consisting instead of thin plates filled with air spaces.
facts.quote: It had little to no cancellous bone, making the centra thin bone plates filled with air spaces

facts.statement: The side walls of Nigersaurus vertebral arches were reduced to 2 mm thick intersecting laminae due to extensive pneumatization.
facts.quote: The vertebral arches were so heavily pierced by extensions of the external air sacs that of their side walls little remained but 2 mm thick intersecting laminae

facts.statement: Unlike the rest of the spine, the tail vertebrae of Nigersaurus had solid centra.
facts.quote: The vertebrae of the tail, however, did have solid centra

facts.statement: The pelvic and pectoral girdle bones of Nigersaurus were very thin, often only several millimeters thick.
facts.quote: The pelvic and pectoral girdle bones were very thin also, often only several millimetres thick

facts.statement: Nigersaurus was initially described by Taquet in 1976 as a dicraeosaurid.
facts.quote: The remains of Nigersaurus were initially described by Taquet in 1976 as belonging to a dicraeosaurid

facts.statement: In 1999, Sereno and colleagues reclassified Nigersaurus as a rebbachisaurid diplodocoid.
facts.quote: but in 1999 Sereno and colleagues reclassified it as a rebbachisaurid diplodocoid

facts.statement: The subfamily Nigersaurinae was named by John A. Whitlock in 2011 to include Nigersaurus and related genera.
facts.quote: The eponymous subfamily Nigersaurinae, which includes Nigersaurus and closely related genera, was named by the American palaeontologist John A. Whitlock in 2011

facts.statement: A 2015 study suggested that Nigersaurinae might be a junior synonym of Rebbachisaurinae.
facts.quote: A 2015 cladistic study by Wilsona and the French palaeontologist Ronan Allain found Rebbachisaurus itself to group with the nigersaurines, and the authors suggested that Nigersaurinae was therefore a junior synonym of Rebbachisaurinae

facts.statement: It is debated whether the clade Rebbachisaurinae necessarily includes Nigersaurus, as some studies place it as a sister taxon to other nigersaurines.
facts.quote: In 2019, Mannion and colleagues pointed out that since Nigersaurus was found to be the sister taxon of all other nigersaurines in some studies, a Rebbachisaurinae clade may not necessarily include Nigersaurus itself

facts.statement: Nigersaurus had an underdeveloped olfactory region and did not possess an advanced sense of smell.
facts.quote: Sereno and colleagues found that Nigersaurus had an underdeveloped olfactory region of its brain and thus did not have an advanced sense of smell

facts.statement: The eyes of Nigersaurus were positioned high on the skull above the muzzle, providing overlapping fields of view.
facts.quote: The eyes of Nigersaurus were placed further towards the top of the skull than in most other sauropods, above the muzzle, which would give it overlapping fields of view

facts.statement: Nigersaurus likely had a visual field close to 360 degrees, requiring hypersensitivity to movement as a prey animal.
facts.quote: Its visual field would have been at or close to 360 degrees, and hypersensitivity of movement would have been important to a vulnerable prey-animal

facts.statement: Ibiricu and colleagues suggested that skeletal pneumaticity in rebbachisaurids was an adaptation to lower skeletal density.
facts.quote: In 2017, the Argentinian palaeontologist Lucio M. Ibiricu and colleagues examined the postcranial skeletal pneumaticity in the skeletons of rebbachisaurids, and suggested that it was an adaptation for lowering the density of the skeleton

facts.statement: Lefebvre and colleagues conducted a 2023 study examining the microanatomical structure of Nigersaurus limb bones using CT-scans.
facts.quote: A 2023 study by the French palaeontologist Rémi Lefebvre and colleagues examined the microanatomical structure of the limb bones of Nigersaurus through CT-scans

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Nigersaurus was a ground-level, non-selective browser.
facts.quote: Nigersaurus was suggested by Sereno and colleagues to be a ground-level, non-selective browser.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus could gather and crop food within 1 meter of the ground surface.
facts.quote: The width of the muzzle and lateral orientation of the tooth row show that the sauropod could gather much food and crop it close to the ground, within 1 m of the surface.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests Nigersaurus had jaw movement limited to precise up-and-down motions.
facts.quote: Nigersaurus also bears signs of low-angle tooth-to-tooth wear on the inside of the maxillary crowns, which suggests that jaw movement was limited to precise up-and-down motions.

facts.statement: A 2011 study indicates Nigersaurus ate relatively soft, herbaceous plants like low-growing ferns.
facts.quote: In addition, according to Whitlock and colleagues in 2011, the small, nearly parallel nature of the tooth scratches and pits (caused by grit, which would not be obtained as often by high-browsers) indicate that it ate relatively soft, herbaceous plants such as low-growing ferns.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus had the highest tooth replacement rate of any known dinosaur.
facts.quote: Nigersaurus wore its tooth crowns down faster than other dinosaurian herbivores, and its tooth replacement rate was the highest of any known dinosaur.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus replaced each tooth approximately every 14 days.
facts.quote: Each tooth was replaced once every 14 days; the rate had previously been estimated lower.

facts.statement: Some researchers suggest Nigersaurus teeth may have functioned like a comb to strain water plants or invertebrates.
facts.quote: Wedel suggested that the evenly spaced teeth of Nigersaurus could have functioned like a comb, by straining water plants or invertebrates, similar to flamingos.
